topic: Day 1 · Post-Renal (Obstructive) AKI — Don't Miss It
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Department of Urology
speakerBio: Urologist with a special interest in emergency decompression and endourology who has never forgiven the phrase 'anuric AKI' in a patient nobody catheterised, and teaches the 'ninety-second bladder scan' rule to every incoming intake.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

An 82-year-old man is admitted overnight "off legs," a bit confused, with a creatinine of 480 µmol/L (baseline 95). The night team labels it "dehydration and sepsis," starts a litre of fluid, and moves on. By morning he is worse, and his creatinine is 560. Nobody has felt his abdomen properly, nobody has looked at his catheter — because he does not have one — and nobody has scanned his bladder. When the day team finally runs a bladder scanner over his suprapubic region it reads 1,100 mL. A catheter drains 1.3 litres of urine, his creatinine falls to 180 within 48 hours, and he walks home. This man did not have "medical" AKI. He had the single most reversible and most missable cause of acute kidney injury — obstruction — and it was nearly missed because the simplest test in medicine was skipped.

1 · 🧭 Why post-renal AKI is the one you cannot afford to miss

Post-renal (obstructive) AKI is caused by a mechanical blockage to urine flow anywhere from the renal pelvis to the urethral meatus. It matters out of all proportion to its frequency for three reasons:

  • It is the fastest fully reversible AKI. Relieve the obstruction and renal function can begin to recover within hours — glomerular filtration resumes almost immediately once back-pressure falls.
  • It is a surgical/urological emergency. The fix is mechanical (a catheter, a nephrostomy, a stent), not medical. Fluids and antibiotics do nothing for a blocked kidney.
  • Prolonged obstruction causes permanent loss. Sustained back-pressure drives tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis; leave it long enough and the nephrons never recover, however perfectly you later decompress.
Obstruction is the most reversible cause of AKI — if you find it in hours. It becomes the most irreversible if you find it in weeks. The clock is the whole game.
💡 The always-scan-the-bladder rule

Every unexplained AKI gets a bladder scan and a renal tract ultrasound, no exceptions. A bladder scan takes ninety seconds, costs nothing, needs no radiology request, and rules the commonest reversible cause in or out at the bedside. If you remember one thing from this talk: you cannot diagnose obstruction you never looked for.

2 · ⚙️ Mechanism — why it takes TWO kidneys (or one lonely one)

Here is the anatomical fact that trips up every foundation-year doctor: to cause AKI, obstruction must block both kidneys — or the single functioning kidney in someone with one working unit. A stone lodged in one ureter of a patient with two healthy kidneys causes agonising renal colic but often a normal creatinine, because the contralateral kidney silently takes up the slack.

So obstructive AKI comes in two anatomical flavours:

LevelRequirement for AKITypical causes
Lower tract (bladder outlet / urethra)A single blockage blocks both kidneys at onceBPH, prostate cancer, urethral stricture, blocked catheter, neurogenic bladder, clot retention
Upper tract (ureters, unilateral)Bilateral disease, OR obstruction of a solitary/single functioning kidneyBilateral stones, bilateral malignant compression, retroperitoneal fibrosis, transitional cell tumour
🎯 The vicious cycle of back-pressure

Obstruction raises the pressure inside the tubule. Rising intratubular pressure opposes glomerular filtration — GFR falls because the hydrostatic gradient across the glomerulus collapses. Sustained high pressure then compresses the medullary vasculature, causing ischaemia; ischaemia and stretch activate the renin–angiotensin system and inflammatory/fibrotic pathways; and within days to weeks the tubulointerstitium scars. Early, filtration is merely "switched off" and switches back on the instant you decompress. Late, the nephron has been remodelled into fibrous tissue and cannot recover. That is why the timeline, not the anatomy, determines the outcome.

3 · 🧱 The causes — a level-by-level differential

Lower tract — the bladder outlet (commonest, especially older men)

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia — the classic cause of chronic retention with acute-on-chronic AKI. Ask about hesitancy, poor stream, nocturia, incomplete emptying.
  • Prostate or bladder malignancy — infiltrating the trigone or urethra.
  • Neurogenic bladder — diabetes, spinal cord disease/injury, cauda equina, multiple sclerosis, anticholinergic and opioid drugs causing atonic high-volume retention.
  • Blocked or misplaced catheter, clot retention, urethral stricture. Always suspect a blocked catheter in an anuric catheterised patient — flush or replace it before you call it "anuric AKI."

Upper tract — the ureters (needs bilateral disease or a solitary kidney)

  • Stones — bilateral, or a stone in a single functioning kidney.
  • Malignancy — pelvic (cervical, bladder, prostate, colorectal), or nodal/retroperitoneal masses compressing both ureters.
  • Retroperitoneal fibrosis — idiopathic (Ormond disease), IgG4-related, drug-related (historically methysergide, ergot derivatives) or malignant; medial deviation of the ureters on imaging is the clue.
  • Papillary necrosis (diabetes, sickle cell, analgesic nephropathy) sloughing into the ureter; iatrogenic ureteric ligation after pelvic surgery.
Anuria is a mechanical word until proven otherwise. Complete anuria means the outflow is blocked, both kidneys have no perfusion, or a cortical catastrophe — and by far the commonest of those is obstruction.
💡 Anuria vs oliguria

Fluctuating or total anuria strongly suggests complete lower-tract obstruction (or a blocked catheter). Intrinsic renal disease and pre-renal AKI almost always leave some urine (oliguria, >100 mL/day). Bilateral complete ureteric obstruction and bilateral renal artery/vein occlusion are the only other true-anuria causes. So a completely dry patient is a bladder scan, not a fluid challenge.

4 · 🖥️ Imaging — scan the bladder, then the tract

TestWhat it answersNotes
Bladder scan (bedside ultrasound)Is there a big post-void residual? (lower-tract obstruction)First-line, instant, no request needed. A high residual → catheterise immediately.
Renal tract ultrasoundIs there hydronephrosis / hydroureter? (upper-tract obstruction)First-line imaging for AKI. Non-invasive, no contrast, no radiation.
CT (non-contrast KUB)Stones, level and cause of obstruction, retroperitoneal masses/RPFBest for stones and for defining the cause when US shows hydronephrosis.
CT urogram / MR urogramAnatomy of malignant or fibrotic obstructionFor planning decompression and staging.
⚠️ Ultrasound can be falsely reassuring — the "no hydro" trap

Hydronephrosis can be absent even with genuine obstruction in three situations: very early obstruction (the collecting system has not yet dilated), a volume-deplete patient (little urine to distend the pelvis), and — critically — obstruction encased by retroperitoneal fibrosis or malignant tumour, where the rigid surrounding tissue physically prevents the pelvicalyceal system from ballooning. If the clinical suspicion of obstruction is high and the ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis, do not stop — proceed to CT. A normal ultrasound does not exclude obstruction.

5 · 🚿 Decompression — the treatment IS mechanical relief

There is no drug for a blocked kidney. Management is to relieve the obstruction at the correct level, urgently, and the choice follows the anatomy:

Level of obstructionDecompressionWho does it
Bladder outlet / urethraUrethral catheter (suprapubic catheter if urethral route impassable)Ward team / urology — do it immediately
Ureter (upper tract)Percutaneous nephrostomy (radiology) or retrograde ureteric stent (JJ) (urology)Interventional radiology / urology

Nephrostomy vs stent — the practical choice

  • Percutaneous nephrostomy — direct drainage into a bag; preferred when the patient is septic/obstructed (infected, obstructed kidney), coagulopathic-permitting, or when retrograde access is impossible. Allows antegrade imaging.
  • Retrograde JJ stent — internalised, more comfortable, no external bag; good for malignant obstruction and where cystoscopic access is straightforward.
⚠️ The obstructed, infected kidney = pyonephrosis = drain it NOW

An obstructed kidney that is also infected is a urological emergency on the level of a surgical abscess: pus under pressure above the blockage, seeding sepsis and destroying the kidney by the hour. Antibiotics cannot sterilise pus behind an obstruction — the only treatment is emergency decompression (usually nephrostomy) alongside antibiotics and resuscitation. Delaying drainage to "let the antibiotics work" or to wait for coagulation results in the morning is how patients go into septic shock and lose the kidney overnight. Obstruction + fever + sepsis = phone urology/IR the same hour.

6 · 💧 Post-obstructive diuresis — the aftermath you must monitor

After you relieve a high-grade obstruction, a substantial fraction of patients develop a post-obstructive diuresis — a large, sometimes torrential urine output (litres per day). Understand the mechanism, because it is part appropriate and part pathological:

  • Appropriate (physiological) component: during obstruction the patient retained salt, water and urea. Once relieved, the kidney offloads this accumulated volume and solute — a natural, self-limiting correction.
  • Pathological component: the obstructed tubules are transiently damaged — they lose their concentrating ability and become resistant to ADH, and retained urea drives an osmotic diuresis. This can continue past the point of euvolaemia and tip the patient into hypovolaemia and dangerous electrolyte loss.

Monitoring and replacement

  • Measure hourly urine output, daily (or twice-daily) weights, and serial U&Es — watch for hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia/hypernatraemia and hypomagnesaemia.
  • Replace fluids judiciously. The trap is to chase output millilitre-for-millilitre, which perpetuates the diuresis by keeping the patient volume-loaded and washing out solute. A common approach is to replace roughly 50–75% of the previous hour's output with a balanced/hypotonic fluid, reassessing volume status clinically, and to let the output taper.
  • Define post-obstructive diuresis by output (e.g. >200 mL/hr for several hours, or >3 L/day) and step down replacement as it settles, usually over 24–72 hours.
Do not match a post-obstructive diuresis litre-for-litre — you will fuel it. Replace a fraction, watch the potassium and magnesium, and let it self-limit.
🎯 Two ways post-obstructive diuresis kills

The first is hypovolaemic collapse in a patient producing 8 litres a day whom nobody is replacing. The second is profound electrolyte depletion — hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia, hypomagnesaemia, and salt wasting — again in an unmonitored patient. Both are entirely preventable with hourly output charting, serial U&Es, and sensible partial replacement. The diuresis itself is expected; the deaths come from not watching it.

7 · 🧑‍⚕️ M&M — the obstructed kidney that was called "sepsis"

☠️ Mortality & Morbidity — the kidney lost to a missed obstruction

A 68-year-old man with known prostate cancer presented with fever, rigors and a creatinine of 320. He was diagnosed with "urosepsis" and started on IV antibiotics and fluids. His flank pain was attributed to "musculoskeletal" and his falling urine output to "acute kidney injury from sepsis." No bladder scan and no ultrasound were performed for 36 hours. When imaging was finally done it showed a right pyonephrosis — an obstructed, infected kidney behind malignant ureteric compression — with a non-functioning left kidney from prior disease. He went into septic shock overnight; an emergency nephrostomy drained frank pus, but he required ICU admission, and the kidney never recovered function — he became dialysis-dependent. Lessons: (1) "urosepsis" with obstruction is obstructed pyonephrosis until excluded — it needs drainage, not just antibiotics; (2) antibiotics cannot treat pus under pressure; (3) any AKI in a patient with pelvic malignancy or prostatism demands an immediate bladder scan and ultrasound; (4) 36 hours of "let's see how the antibiotics do" cost this man his only working kidney. The single missing action was a ninety-second bladder scan on admission.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Always scan the bladder and image the renal tract in every unexplained AKI — obstruction is the reversible cause you can only find if you look.
  2. Obstruction causes AKI only when it blocks both kidneys — bilateral disease, bladder-outlet obstruction, or a single functioning kidney.
  3. It is the fastest reversible AKI if relieved in hours, and the most irreversible if left for weeks — the clock decides the outcome.
  4. Ultrasound can be falsely negative in early, volume-deplete, or tumour/RPF-encased obstruction — if suspicion is high and there's no hydronephrosis, get a CT.
  5. Treatment is mechanical: catheter for outlet obstruction; nephrostomy or JJ stent for ureteric obstruction.
  6. An obstructed, infected kidney (pyonephrosis) is a same-hour emergency — emergency decompression plus antibiotics; antibiotics alone will not sterilise pus under pressure.
  7. Anticipate post-obstructive diuresis: monitor hourly output, weights and serial U&Es, replace a fraction (not litre-for-litre), and watch potassium and magnesium.
  8. Complete anuria is a mechanical diagnosis — think blocked catheter or complete obstruction first, not a fluid challenge.

moderatorQs.q: Why does a single ureteric stone rarely cause a rise in creatinine, and when should a stone actually worry you about AKI?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because obstruction only causes AKI when it compromises both kidneys' worth of nephrons. A stone lodged in one ureter of a patient with two normal kidneys produces severe renal colic but the contralateral kidney compensates, so the creatinine often stays normal. A stone becomes an AKI emergency when there is bilateral obstruction, or when it obstructs a single functioning kidney (a solitary kidney, or one where the other is already non-functioning from prior disease). The other scenario that turns a stone into a same-hour emergency is an obstructed, infected kidney — stone plus fever and sepsis — which is a pyonephrosis needing emergency decompression regardless of the creatinine.

moderatorQs.q: The ultrasound in a patient you strongly suspect is obstructed shows no hydronephrosis. Does that exclude obstruction?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No. Hydronephrosis can be genuinely absent in three important situations: very early obstruction (the collecting system has not had time to dilate), a volume-deplete patient (insufficient urine to distend the pelvis), and obstruction encased by retroperitoneal fibrosis or malignant tumour, where the rigid surrounding tissue physically prevents the pelvicalyceal system from ballooning. If clinical suspicion remains high despite a 'no hydro' ultrasound, the correct move is to proceed to CT rather than accept the negative scan. A normal ultrasound reduces but does not eliminate the probability of obstruction.

moderatorQs.q: Explain post-obstructive diuresis and how you would manage a patient producing 400 mL an hour after catheterisation.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Post-obstructive diuresis has a physiological component — offloading the salt, water and urea retained during obstruction — and a pathological component — transiently damaged tubules that cannot concentrate urine, are ADH-resistant, and lose salt, compounded by a urea-driven osmotic diuresis. At 400 mL/hr I would not replace litre-for-litre, which perpetuates the diuresis; instead I'd monitor hourly urine output, daily weights and serial U&Es, replace roughly 50–75% of output with a balanced/hypotonic fluid while reassessing volume status clinically, and aggressively watch for and replace potassium and magnesium losses. The diuresis is expected and self-limiting over 24–72 hours; the danger is unmonitored hypovolaemia and electrolyte depletion, both preventable.

audienceQs.q: A catheterised patient on the ward has become anuric. What's my first move before I bleep about 'anuric AKI'?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Assume the catheter is blocked until you have proven otherwise — it is far commoner than true anuric renal failure. Flush the catheter with saline and, if it does not drain freely, replace it. Complete anuria is a mechanical word: it means the outflow is blocked, both kidneys have lost perfusion, or a cortical catastrophe — and the commonest of those on a ward is obstruction, often just a blocked or kinked catheter or clot retention. A bladder scan will show whether the bladder is full (outlet/catheter problem) or empty (upstream problem). Sort the plumbing before you escalate as 'renal failure'.

audienceQs.q: My patient has AKI with fever and a stone obstructing one kidney. Can I just treat with antibiotics and arrange decompression electively tomorrow?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — an obstructed, infected kidney (pyonephrosis) is an emergency needing decompression the same hour, alongside antibiotics and resuscitation. Behind the obstruction is pus under pressure that antibiotics cannot reach or sterilise; leaving it overnight risks fulminant septic shock and irreversible loss of that kidney. Contact urology and interventional radiology urgently — usually a percutaneous nephrostomy (preferred in the septic, obstructed kidney) or a retrograde ureteric stent. Do not delay drainage to 'let the antibiotics work' or to wait for morning; source control here is mechanical and it is time-critical.

audienceQs.q: What's the single most useful first-line imaging for suspected obstructive AKI, and when do we go to CT?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The first-line pair is a bedside bladder scan (for a large post-void residual = lower-tract obstruction) and a renal tract ultrasound (for hydronephrosis/hydroureter = upper-tract obstruction) — both non-invasive, no contrast, no radiation. Go to CT (non-contrast KUB for stones, or CT/MR urogram for anatomy) when the ultrasound shows hydronephrosis and you need to define the level and cause, when stones are suspected, or — importantly — when clinical suspicion of obstruction is high despite a normal ultrasound, because hydronephrosis can be falsely absent in early, volume-deplete, or tumour/retroperitoneal-fibrosis-encased obstruction.
